extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, journalists, and lawyers seeking an overview of defamation law
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive encyclopedic overview of defamation (libel and slander), describing its definition, elements, defences, remedies, human-rights balancing, and jurisdictional variations across common law, civil law, and other legal traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of defamation
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation is a communication that injures a third party's reputation and causes a legally redressable injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The precise legal definition varies by country; it is not necessarily restricted to false assertions and can extend to concepts more abstract than reputation such as dignity and honour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between libel and slander
rubrics_metrics.description: Libel refers to defamation in written, printed, posted online, or broadcast form; slander refers to oral speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fundamental distinction lies in the form in which defamatory matter is published; broadcast spoken statements may be treated as libel in some jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil vs criminal treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation may be treated as a civil wrong (tort/delict), a criminal offence, or both depending on jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies and penalties differ accordingly; many jurisdictions historically used criminal penalties, but trends and human-rights bodies advise caution and decriminalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-rights balancing (ICCPR Article 17 and 19)
rubrics_metrics.description: Right to protection against unlawful attacks on honour and reputation (Article 17 ICCPR) co-exists with right to freedom of expression (Article 19 ICCPR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domestic defamation law should balance individuals' right to protect reputation with freedom of expression and of the press; Article 19 allows restrictions necessary 'for respect of the rights or reputations of others.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-part test for permissible restrictions (UN Human Rights Committee)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations on expression must be (1) provided by law that is clear and accessible, (2) necessary and legitimate to protect rights/reputations, and (3) proportionate and the least restrictive means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This three-part test is analogous to domestic proportionality tests (e.g., Oakes Test in Canada) and is used by courts when assessing whether defamation restrictions are justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: General comment No. 34 guidance on defamation laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation laws must be crafted to comply with freedom of expression protections and should not be used to stifle expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically: include defences such as truth; avoid applying to expressions not subject to verification; consider avoiding penalizing honest errors about public figures; recognize public interest as a defence; avoid excessive penalties; consider decriminalization; imprisonment is never appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies in defamation actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful plaintiffs may obtain remedies such as damages, injunctions to stop publication, corrections, retractions, or apologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Available remedies vary by jurisdiction; some jurisdictions also allow punitive damages in flagrant cases or other jurisdiction-specific remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-law elements of defamation (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: To constitute defamation, a claim must generally be false and published to someone other than the person defamed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some jurisdictions require additional elements such as proof of damages; others recognize special rules for public-figure statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact vs opinion doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Only false statements of fact (as opposed to opinion) can be defamatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements of opinion are inherently non-falsifiable and therefore generally not actionable; the distinction is central to defences such as opinion and truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth (justification) defence
rubrics_metrics.description: Proving the truth of an allegedly defamatory statement is always a valid defence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some jurisdictions partial truth may suffice if unproven allegations do not materially injure the claimant's reputation (statutory or doctrinal variants exist).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial truth doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement is not defamatory if it is substantially true despite slight inaccuracies of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. doctrine allows slight inaccuracies so long as the 'gist' or 'sting' of the statement is true; some Commonwealth statutes provide similar relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest / responsible publication defence
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-founded public interest in the information may provide a defence to defamation, including for public figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public interest is 'what is in the interest of the public', not merely what the public is curious about; jurisdictions (e.g., Canada) recognize 'responsible communication' defences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privilege (absolute and qualified)
rubrics_metrics.description: Privilege is a circumstance that justifies or excuses otherwise actionable statements—absolute privilege provides complete protection; qualified privilege is conditional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: absolute privilege for statements in court or parliamentary proceedings; qualified privilege for reporting on public meetings or matters of public interest, sometimes applying to journalists subject to conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistake of fact defence
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements made in good faith and with a reasonable belief in their truth may be treated the same as true statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may scrutinize the reasonableness of the belief; the degree of care expected may vary by the defendant's role (e.g., media expected to check multiple sources).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere vulgar abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Insults or vituperative statements not intended to be taken literally or likely to cause real damage are not necessarily defamatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: angry insults during arguments that a reasonable person would not regard as factual assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair comment (honest opinion on public interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements made with an honest belief on matters of public interest are protected even if logically unsound, provided a reasonable person could hold that opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects criticisms of official acts and matters of public concern when honestly held as opinion rather than asserted as fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent defence
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the plaintiff consented to the dissemination of the statement, a defamation claim may be barred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used rarely and fact-specific; consent must be demonstrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innocent dissemination defence
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant is not liable if they had no actual knowledge of the defamatory statement or no reason to believe it was defamatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to intermediaries such as delivery services or distributors; can be defeated if lack of knowledge resulted from negligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incapability of further defamation / 'libel-proof' plaintiff
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claimant's reputation is already so poor that further statements cannot harm it, no defamation remedy may lie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically recognized as a defence in some jurisdictions where actual damage is an essential element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of limitations / timing of publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Most jurisdictions require lawsuits to be brought within a limited period; for mass media or internet publications the limitation runs from publication date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute lengths and accrual rules vary by jurisdiction; discovery-based accrual may be limited for mass publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of third-party communication
rubrics_metrics.description: If no one other than the plaintiff and defendant heard the statement, there is no actionable defamation (no publication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private accusations in isolated contexts without dissemination typically do not give rise to defamation claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of actual injury (verifiable reputational harm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even with third-party communication, if the third party does not believe or care about the statement, there is no injury and thus no recourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some jurisdictions presume injury for certain categories (defamation per se), while others require proof of actual damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media liability and defamation insurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers and journalists often purchase insurance to cover potential libel damages and legal costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice includes buying worldwide coverage and recognizing that investigative journalism often attracts higher premiums or coverage exclusions; a significant share of insurer payouts go to legal costs rather than settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation per se categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain false statements are so damaging that they create a presumption of injury (defamation per se).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commonly recognized categories: accusing someone of a crime; alleging they have a loathsome disease; statements harming fitness to conduct business or profession; imputing serious sexual misconduct. If proved false, no need to prove special damages though truth is still a defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: United States specific elements and fault rules
rubrics_metrics.description: In the U.S., a plaintiff typically must show: a false and defamatory statement concerning the plaintiff; publication to a third party; at least negligence for matters of public concern; and damages. Public figures or officials must also prove 'actual malice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The actual malice standard (New York Times Co. v. Sullivan) requires showing the publisher knew the statement was false or acted with reckless disregard for the truth; state variations and statutory rules apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual malice standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A heightened fault standard applicable to public officials and public figures in U.S. libel law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined as publishing with knowledge of falsity or with reckless disregard for whether the statement was true or false; established by New York Times Co. v. Sullivan (1964).

rubrics_metrics.name: SLAPPs and procedural protective measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategic lawsuits against public participation (SLAPPs) have prompted tort-reform measures allowing expedited motions to strike or dismiss and suspension of discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include California's special motion to strike and Ontario's Protection of Public Participation Act; successful motions may terminate lawsuits and permit recovery of costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate defamation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdictions differ on corporate standing in defamation suits and required proof of harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Australia generally denies private corporations the right to sue (except small businesses); Canada grants corporations similar rights as individuals; England (since 2013) allows private corporations to sue but requires proof of serious harm and serious financial loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roman Dutch / Scots 'actio iniuriarum' elements
rubrics_metrics.description: In jurisdictions applying Roman Dutch law and in Scots law, liability arises under actio iniuriarum requiring harm (violation of personality interests), wrongful conduct, and intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harm encompasses infringements of 'corpus', 'dignitas', or 'fama'; Scots law emphasizes contumelia and often allows veritas (truth) as the chief defence; negligent interference with dignitary interests may not suffice for liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal defamation considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions treat defamation as a criminal offence with potential penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human-rights bodies advise careful crafting of criminal defamation laws, recommending defences such as truth, decriminalization where possible, avoiding excessive penalties, and that imprisonment is never appropriate; Article 19 advocacy groups map global criminal defamation laws.
